intro.title: Money without a quarrel
paragraphs: Shared expenses are split unevenly, and it’s building up. Talking about it feels awkward: you’re afraid of offending them or starting a row.
You try to discuss it so that you find a solution, not a winner.
Choose what to say. If an answer doesn’t work, you stay where you are, see the reaction and understand why.
intro.note: The other person’s styles are patterns of behaviour, not types of people: the same person acts differently on different days. Real people react differently, so this is practice with wording, not a prediction.
intro.disclaimer: A learning simulation. The material draws on well-known communication methods (sources are given at each step), but it has not yet been reviewed by a psychologist.

variants.name: Defensive, irritable
variants.desc: Quickly hears blame and gets defensive.

variants.name: Avoids the topic
variants.desc: Puts off the conversation, feels shy, worries silently.

nodes.narr: An evening in the kitchen. You need to discuss shared expenses: over the last few months your contributions have been uneven.

options.text: I’d like to calmly discuss our shared expenses so it’s clear and fair for both of us. When suits you: now or tomorrow evening?
options.why: A “soft start-up” without blame and with a choice of time lowers the other person’s defences. The topic sounds like a shared task, not a complaint.

direct.say: Let’s do it now, since we’ve started. I’m listening.

evasive.say: Let’s do tomorrow evening. Good that I get a choice.

options.text: We urgently need to talk about money, you’re spending everything again.
options.why: Blame and “urgently” trigger defensiveness. The talk turns into an argument about character, not expenses.

direct.say: Here we go again.

evasive.say: Here it comes. I don’t want to hear it.

options.text: Everything’s become so expensive, hasn’t it?
options.why: A hint leaves the other person guessing what you want. A hidden reproach is heard as an accusation.

direct.say: What are you getting at?

evasive.say: Do you want to say something? Say it straight.

options.text: Oh, nothing, everything’s fine. We’ll sort it out sometime.
options.why: Built-up resentment will grow and burst out later, at the worst moment. Better to talk before it builds up.

direct.say: Say nothing? OK.

evasive.say: OK, as you say.

tech.name: A soft start to the conversation
tech.src: Gottman & Silver, «The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work», 1999
tech.text: Starting with a description of the problem, without blame and with respect, makes a constructive outcome more likely.

nodes.hint: How to start so the other person doesn’t get defensive?

direct.say: Did something happen? You look serious.

evasive.say: Not today, please, I’m tired.

nodes.narr: The other person is ready to listen.
nodes.ask: How do you describe the situation?

options.text: Over the last three months shared expenses averaged 60 thousand. My share was about 40, yours about 20. I want to work out how we can make it more even.
options.why: Facts without judgements (numbers, not character) let you discuss the problem together. You describe instead of accusing.

direct.say: Hm, that’s right. I didn’t think the difference was that big.

evasive.say: I didn’t count it was that much. Let’s look.

options.text: You don’t think about money at all, almost all the payments are on me.
options.why: The generalisation “at all” and the label “you don’t think” trigger defensiveness. And “it’s all on me” sounds like a martyr’s position.

direct.say: That’s unfair. I contribute too.

evasive.say: You see, you’re blaming me.

options.text: And last year it was exactly the same.
options.why: Going back to old episodes distracts from the current problem and heats up the conversation.

direct.say: What does last year have to do with it?

evasive.say: You’re digging up the past again.

options.text: Well, money isn’t really working out somehow…
options.why: A vague description gives nothing to hold on to. The other person doesn’t understand what the talk is about.

direct.say: I don’t get it. More specifically?

evasive.say: What exactly isn’t working?

tech.name: Describe without judging
tech.text: Describe facts anyone could see: numbers, dates, actions. Leave judgements and labels out.

nodes.hint: What here is a fact anyone can see, and what is a judgement?

direct.say: Go on then, what is it.

evasive.say: OK, go ahead. Just no reproaches.

nodes.narr: The other person answers and explains their side.

options.text: You didn’t want to burden me, and because of that it was hard for you on your own. Do I understand right?
options.why: Reflecting what you heard shows you understood the reason. It eases the tension and opens the way to a solution.

direct.say: Yes, roughly. Thanks for hearing me.

evasive.say: Yes… I felt awkward. Thanks for hearing me.

options.text: You should have said so right away, not hidden it.
options.why: Advice with a reproach brings back guilt. First understand, then look for solutions.

direct.say: So now it’s my fault too.

evasive.say: I already feel ashamed, don’t add to it.

options.text: OK, it’s nothing, forget it.
options.why: Dismissing it closes the topic, and the imbalance will stay. The other person hears: “I’m not interested”.

direct.say: To you it’s nothing, but I was worried.

evasive.say: If it’s nothing, why are we talking?

options.text: I had unexpected expenses too, so we’re in the same boat.
options.why: Being open in return is fine, but first show that you heard them. Otherwise it looks like a counter-argument.

direct.say: Well, it happens to you too. OK.

evasive.say: OK, so it’s hard for both of us.

tech.name: Reflecting feelings
tech.text: Say in your own words what you heard and ask if it’s right. This lowers defences and clarifies the reason.

nodes.hint: What to do before looking for a solution?

direct.say: I had unexpected expenses, and I didn’t want to tell you so as not to burden you.

evasive.say: I was too embarrassed to say my income is lower for now.

nodes.narr: You both see the picture. Now suggest how to split the expenses.

options.text: Let’s contribute in proportion to income: each of us pays our share of the total. If that doesn’t suit you, we can come up with another option together.
options.why: A specific proposal plus willingness to look for another: you name an option and leave room for a joint decision. This is the principle of interests instead of positions.

direct.say: In proportion… That’s fair. Let’s work it out.

evasive.say: That’s fair. Let’s work it out together.

options.text: Half and half, and that’s it.
options.why: A rigid position that ignores the difference in income brings pushback or formal agreement with resentment behind it.

direct.say: That doesn’t suit me. Let’s discuss.

evasive.say: If it’s half and half, I can’t manage.

options.text: You just need to pay more.
options.why: An ultimatum without discussion closes the dialogue. The decision should be shared.

direct.say: Don’t order me around.

evasive.say: Are you telling me what to do?

options.text: Let’s think more and discuss it later.
options.why: Postponing without a date leaves the problem unsolved. Deadlines are needed so the topic doesn’t dissolve.

direct.say: “Later” again?

evasive.say: OK, let’s think. Although it’s being put off again.

tech.name: Interests instead of positions
tech.text: Discuss what matters to each of you and look for an option where both sides win.

nodes.hint: How to propose a specific solution without closing the discussion?

direct.say: And what do you suggest?

evasive.say: Just don’t complicate things. What do you want?

nodes.narr: There’s an agreement; now it needs locking in.
nodes.ask: How do you lock it in?

options.text: Let’s pay our shares from the first of the month and check in a month whether it works for us. I’ll set a reminder.
options.why: A specific date and a check-in turn an intention into a plan. A review after a month removes the fear of “forever”.

direct.say: OK, from the first. And we’ll check in.

evasive.say: Deal. Remind me a couple of days before.

options.text: The main thing is that it doesn’t happen again.
options.why: A general phrase sets no actions and sounds like a reproach. You need specific steps and a date.

direct.say: Yeah, it won’t happen again.

evasive.say: OK, I’ll try.

options.text: Good, then we won’t talk about it again.
options.why: Closing the topic “for good” leaves no room for adjustment. If the scheme doesn’t work, it will be awkward to bring it up again.

direct.say: Well, as you say.

evasive.say: OK.

options.text: Thanks for the talk.
options.why: Thanks matter. Stronger: add a date — when exactly you start and when you check in.

direct.say: You’re welcome. Let’s pin down the dates.

evasive.say: Thanks. Let’s write down the dates.

tech.name: A specific “if–then” plan
tech.text: Decide when and how exactly it will be done. Specific plans increase the chance of follow-through.

nodes.hint: What will make the agreement real?

direct.say: OK, let’s do that.

evasive.say: Fine. Let’s just not forget.

direct.say: Let’s start from the first. Good that we talked.

evasive.say: Good. I feel calmer now.

finale.title: Money without a quarrel
finale.lead: The conversation started softly, stayed with the facts and ended with a dated plan. Here’s what it relied on:
carry: Starting without blame and offering a choice of time.
Speaking in numbers and facts, not labels.
Hearing first, proposing second; locking it in with a date.
finale.prompt: What do you want to agree on about money? Write down the first sentence.
